--- title: "6.4 Poisson Regression Example" --- ## Software considerations - Convergence (of the maximum likelihood estimates) is usually fast and problems are rarely encountered - Also true for negative binomial model (covered next) - Convergence can be trickier for zero-inflated count models (covered end of this section) - But, lack of convergence generally indicates that model is not a good fit for your data and solution is to use a regular count model ## Example - Add Health Wave IV - DV: Number of drinks consumed in a typical sitting - IVs: Gender, Age (24 -- 33) - Controls: Education, race, income, marital status, parental status ::: {.panel-tabset group="language"} ## Stata ```{.stata-run} . use "https://tdmize.github.io/data/data/cda_ah4", clear (cda_ah4.dta | Add Health Wave 4 - | ) . . *6.4.a . hist drinktime, percent fcolor(none) xlab(0(2)18) /// > title("[6.4.a] Distribution of Number of Drinks Consumed in a Typical Sitt > ing") (bin=37, start=0, width=.48648649) ``` ![](fig/cda-06_04_a-drinks-01.png){width=80% fig-alt="[6.4.a] Histogram of the average number of drinks in a sitting, from 0 to 18: about 42% report 0 drinks, about 10% 1, 15% 2, 11% 3, and few report more than 6."} ## R ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} library(haven) # import Stata data and labels library(dplyr) # data manipulation library(ggplot2) # graphs library(modelsummary) # regression tables library(marginaleffects) # predictions and marginal effects library(cleanplots) # graph scheme cleanplots_defaults() ah4 <- read_dta("https://tdmize.github.io/data/data/cda_ah4.dta") # 6.4.a ggplot(ah4, aes(x = drinktime)) + geom_histogram(aes(y = after_stat(100 * count / sum(count))), binwidth = 1, fill = NA, color = "black") + scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(0, 18, 2)) + labs(title = "[6.4.a] Distribution of Number of Drinks Consumed in a Typical Sitting", x = "Average Drinks Each Time", y = "Percent") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](6-4-poisson-example_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-1-1.png){fig-alt='[6.4.a] Histogram of the average number of drinks in a sitting, from 0 to 18: about 42% report 0 drinks, about 10% 1, 15% 2, 11% 3, and few report more than 6.' width=80%} ::: ::: ::: ::: {.panel-tabset group="language"} ## Stata ```{.stata-run} . *6.4.b . poisson drinktime i.woman c.age i.college i.race c.income /// > i.spouserole i.parrole Iteration 0: Log likelihood = -11915.53 Iteration 1: Log likelihood = -11915.529 Poisson regression Number of obs = 4,983 LR chi2(9) = 1610.51 Prob > chi2 = 0.0000 Log likelihood = -11915.529 Pseudo R2 = 0.0633 ------------------------------------------------------------------------------- drinktime | Coefficient Std. err. z P>|z| [95% conf. interval] --------------+---------------------------------------------------------------- woman | Woman | -0.496 0.021 -23.208 0.000 -0.538 -0.454 age | -0.051 0.005 -9.265 0.000 -0.061 -0.040 | college | College De.. | -0.253 0.023 -10.869 0.000 -0.298 -0.207 | race | Black | -0.367 0.026 -14.069 0.000 -0.418 -0.316 Native Ame.. | 0.286 0.093 3.085 0.002 0.104 0.467 Asian | -0.132 0.058 -2.282 0.023 -0.246 -0.019 | income | 0.003 0.000 7.931 0.000 0.002 0.004 | spouserole | Married | -0.131 0.022 -6.065 0.000 -0.173 -0.089 | parrole | Parent | -0.225 0.023 -9.697 0.000 -0.271 -0.180 _cons | 2.642 0.154 17.153 0.000 2.340 2.944 ------------------------------------------------------------------------------- . est store pmod . est table pmod, /// > title("[6.4.b] Poisson regression for # of drinks in a sitting") /// > b(%5.3f) star(.05 .01 .001) [6.4.b] Poisson regression for # of drinks in a sitting --------------------------- Variable | pmod -------------+------------- woman | Woman | -0.496*** age | -0.051*** | college | College D.. | -0.253*** | race | Black | -0.367*** Native Am.. | 0.286** Asian | -0.132* | income | 0.003*** | spouserole | Married | -0.131*** | parrole | Parent | -0.225*** _cons | 2.642*** --------------------------- Legend: * p<.05; ** p<.01; *** p<.001 ``` ## R ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # Keep model variables; drop any missing data ah4 <- ah4[c("drinktime", "woman", "age", "college", "race", "income", "spouserole", "parrole")] ah4 <- ah4[complete.cases(ah4), ] # Treat binary/nominal variables as factors ah4 <- ah4 |> mutate(across(c(woman, college, race, spouserole, parrole), as_factor)) # 6.4.b pmod <- glm(drinktime ~ woman + age + college + race + income + spouserole + parrole, family = "poisson", data = ah4) modelsummary(pmod, stars = c("*" = .05, "**" = .01, "***" = .001), title = "[6.4.b] Poisson regression for # of drinks in a sitting") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ```{=html}

``` ::: ::: ::: ::: {.callout-note icon="false" appearance="simple"} In Stata, use the [**poisson**](https://www.stata.com/manuals13/rpoisson.pdf) command In R, use [**glm**](https://www.rdocumentation.org/packages/stats/versions/3.6.2/topics/glm) and specify family = "poisson" Poisson regression coefficients are in the metric of the log rate---which is not very useful We usually exponentiate the coefficients and interpret in terms of the factor change on the rate (see below) ::: ## Factor change in the rate E(y | x) - To go from log rates to rates metric, we exponentiate the coefficients - This makes the coefficients multiplicative effects - The effect of a change in *x~k~* does not depend on values of the *x*'s > ***Factor change interpretation**: For a unit change in x~k~ the expected count (rate) changes by a factor of exp(β~k~), holding other variables constant* ### Interpreting factor changes in rate ::: {.panel-tabset group="language"} ## Stata ```{.stata-run} . *6.4.c - Exponentiated coefs with irr option . qui poisson drinktime i.woman c.age i.college i.race c.income /// > i.spouserole i.parrole, irr . est table pmod, /// > title("[6.4.c] Poisson regression for # of drinks in a sitting (exponentia > ted coefficients = IRRs)") /// > b(%5.3f) star(.05 .01 .001) eform [6.4.c] Poisson regression for # of drinks in a sitting (exponentiated coefficients = IRRs) --------------------------- Variable | pmod -------------+------------- woman | Woman | 0.609*** age | 0.951*** | college | College D.. | 0.777*** | race | Black | 0.693*** Native Am.. | 1.330** Asian | 0.876* | income | 1.003*** | spouserole | Married | 0.877*** | parrole | Parent | 0.798*** _cons | 14.040*** --------------------------- Legend: * p<.05; ** p<.01; *** p<.001 ``` ## R ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # 6.4.c - Exponentiated coefficients exp(coef(pmod)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` r-output (Intercept) womanWoman age collegeCollege Degree 14.0395911 0.6089678 0.9506264 0.7766083 raceBlack raceNative American raceAsian income 0.6929874 1.3304467 0.8761973 1.0028888 spouseroleMarried parroleParent 0.8772996 0.7981304 ``` ::: ::: ::: ::: {.callout-note icon="false" appearance="simple"} Exponentiated coefficients are referred to as "incident rate ratios" in Poisson ::: > - *Women's rates of drinking are lower than men's by a factor of about 0.61* > - *Each additional year of age is associated with a 0.95 times decrease in the number of drinks consumed in a sitting* > - *Black and Asian respondents drink fewer drinks in a sitting than do White respondents (e^b^ = 0.69; e^b^ = 0.88); in contrast, Native American respondents drink 1.33 times more drinks in a sitting than White respondents* > - *An additional \$1000 of income is associated with consuming 1.003 times more drinks in a sitting* ## Plots of the predicted rate - The predicted rate is the default quantity with **margins** in Stata and with **plot_predictions** in R - Easy to calculate $$E(y) = \widehat{\mu} = \exp(\mathbf{x}\boldsymbol{\beta})$$ ::: {.panel-tabset group="language"} ## Stata ```{.stata-run} . *6.4.e . qui margins, at(age=(24(1)33) woman=(0 1)) . marginsplot, recastci(rline) ciopts(lpat(dash) col(gs12)) ylab(0(1)4) /// > ytitle("Number of Drinks") xtitle("Age in Years") /// > title("[6.4.e] Predicted Number of Drinks in a Typical Sitting Based on Ag > e", size(medium)) Variables that uniquely identify margins: age woman ``` ![](fig/cda-06_04_e-drinks-06.png){width=80% fig-alt="[6.4.e] Predicted number of drinks in a sitting by age, with confidence intervals: men's predictions fall from about 3.3 at age 24 to 2.1 at age 33, and women's from about 2.0 to 1.3."} ## R ::: {.callout-note icon="false" appearance="simple"} R's **plot_predictions** default would hold controls at modal person. To get average predictions, need the **newdata** statement with a "counterfactual" **grid_type.** ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # 6.4.e plot_predictions(pmod, by = c("age", "woman"), newdata = datagrid(age = 24:33, woman = unique, grid_type = "counterfactual")) + scale_x_continuous(breaks = 24:33) + scale_y_continuous(breaks = 0:4, limits = c(0, 4)) + labs(title = "[6.4.e] Predicted Number of Drinks in a Typical Sitting Based on Age", x = "Age in Years", y = "Number of Drinks", color = NULL, fill = NULL) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](6-4-poisson-example_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-4-1.png){fig-alt='[6.4.e] Predicted number of drinks in a sitting by age, with confidence intervals: men\'s predictions fall from about 3.3 at age 24 to 2.1 at age 33, and women\'s from about 2.0 to 1.3.' width=80%} ::: ::: ::: ::: {.panel-tabset group="language"} ## Stata ```{.stata-run} . *6.4.f . qui margins, at(income=(0(5)150) woman=(0 1)) . marginsplot, recastci(rline) ciopts(lpat(dash) col(gs12)) ylab(0(1)4) xlab(0(2 > 5)150) /// > plotopts(msym(i)) /// > ytitle("Number of Drinks") xtitle("Personal Income in $1000s") /// > title("[6.4.f] Predicted Number of Drinks in a Typical Sitting Based on In > come", size(medium)) Variables that uniquely identify margins: income woman ``` ![](fig/cda-06_04_f-drinks-08.png){width=80% fig-alt="[6.4.f] Predicted number of drinks in a sitting by personal income, with confidence intervals: men's predictions rise from about 2.4 at no income to 3.7 at $150,000, and women's from about 1.5 to 2.3."} ## R ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # 6.4.f plot_predictions(pmod, by = c("income", "woman"), newdata = datagrid(income = seq(0, 150, 5), woman = unique, grid_type = "counterfactual")) + scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(0, 150, 25)) + scale_y_continuous(breaks = 0:4) + coord_cartesian(ylim = c(0, 4)) + labs(title = "[6.4.f] Predicted Number of Drinks in a Typical Sitting Based on Income", x = "Personal Income in $1000s", y = "Number of Drinks", color = NULL, fill = NULL) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](6-4-poisson-example_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-5-1.png){fig-alt='[6.4.f] Predicted number of drinks in a sitting by personal income, with confidence intervals: men\'s predictions rise from about 2.4 at no income to 3.7 at $150,000, and women\'s from about 1.5 to 2.3.' width=80%} ::: ::: ::: ### Marginal effects on rates are not constant ::: {.panel-tabset group="language"} ## Stata ```{.stata-run} . *Show nonlinearities (predictions across a broader range) . *6.4.g . qui margins, at(age=(0(2.5)100)) . marginsplot, noci xlab(0(20)100) ylab(0(2)10) plotopts(msym(i)) /// > ytitle("Number of Drinks") xtitle("Age in Years") /// > title("[6.4.g] Predicted Number of Drinks in a Typical Sitting Based on Ag > e", size(medium)) Variables that uniquely identify margins: age . *6.4.h . qui margins, at(income=(0(50)2000)) . marginsplot, noci ylab() xlab(0(250)2000) /// > plotopts(msym(i)) /// > ytitle("Number of Drinks") xtitle("Personal Income in $1000s") /// > title("[6.4.h] Predicted Number of Drinks in a Typical Sitting Based on In > come", size(medium)) Variables that uniquely identify margins: income ``` ![](fig/cda-06_04_g-drinks-07.png){width=80% fig-alt="[6.4.g] Predicted number of drinks by age from 0 to 100, far beyond the observed ages: the curve falls steeply from about 9 at age 0 and flattens near 0 by age 80, showing the exponential form of the model."} ![](fig/cda-06_04_h-drinks-09.png){width=80% fig-alt="[6.4.h] Predicted number of drinks by personal income from 0 to $2,000,000, far beyond the observed incomes: the curve is nearly flat at first and then rises steeply to about 600 drinks, showing the exponential form of the model."} ## R ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # Show nonlinearities (predictions across a broader range) # 6.4.g plot_predictions(pmod, by = "age", newdata = datagrid(age = seq(0, 100, 2.5), grid_type = "counterfactual"), vcov = FALSE) + scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(0, 100, 20)) + scale_y_continuous(breaks = seq(0, 10, 2), limits = c(0, 10)) + labs(title = "[6.4.g] Predicted Number of Drinks in a Typical Sitting Based on Age", x = "Age in Years", y = "Number of Drinks") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](6-4-poisson-example_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-6-1.png){fig-alt='[6.4.g] Predicted number of drinks by age from 0 to 100, far beyond the observed ages: the curve falls steeply from about 9 at age 0 and flattens near 0 by age 80, showing the exponential form of the model.' width=80%} ::: ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # 6.4.h plot_predictions(pmod, by = "income", newdata = datagrid(income = seq(0, 2000, 50), grid_type = "counterfactual"), vcov = FALSE) + scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(0, 2000, 250)) + labs(title = "[6.4.h] Predicted Number of Drinks in a Typical Sitting Based on Income", x = "Personal Income in $1000s", y = "Number of Drinks") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](6-4-poisson-example_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-7-1.png){fig-alt='[6.4.h] Predicted number of drinks by personal income from 0 to $2,000,000, far beyond the observed incomes: the curve is nearly flat at first and then rises steeply to about 600 drinks, showing the exponential form of the model.' width=80%} ::: ::: ::: ## Marginal effect on the rate - The factor change (*e^b^*) is constant; it does not differ across values of the IVs - The marginal effect depends on the values of the IVs - Considerations about what starting and ending values to use; whether to hold control variables at the mean (MEM) or to average over observed values (AMEs) are identical in count models to other nonlinear models $$ME = \eta(x_{k} = end,\, \mathbf{x}_{-k} = \mathbf{x}^{*}) - \eta(x_{k} = start,\, \mathbf{x}_{-k} = \mathbf{x}^{*})$$ - There are multiple potential predictions of interest with count models - Can define $\eta$ as the rate (AKA expected count; AKA \# of expected "events") - Can define $\eta$ as the Pr(*y* = *j*) - Can define $\eta$ as the probability of a range of outcomes, e.g., Pr(*y* = 4,5,6,7, or 8) - For marginal effects on the rate/count: > ***Interpretation:** The difference in the expected count for a change in x~k~ of δ, holding other independent variables constant* ::: {.panel-tabset group="language"} ## Stata ```{.stata-run} . mecompare woman, model(pmod) Predicting: Predicted number of events Marginal effects (N_pmod=4983) | ME # Estimate SE P>|z| ---------------------------------+--------------------------------------- woman | Woman - Man | pmod | 1 -1.038 0.045 0.000 ``` ## R ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} avg_comparisons(pmod, variables = "woman") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` r-output Estimate Std. Error z Pr(>|z|) S 2.5 % 97.5 % -1.04 0.0447 -23.2 <0.001 393.8 -1.13 -0.95 Term: woman Type: response Comparison: Woman - Man ``` ::: ::: ::: > *On average, women consume about one fewer drink in a typical sitting than do men (ME = -1.038; p \< 0.001).* ::: {.callout-note icon="false" appearance="simple"} **Interpretation tip**: Count DVs tend to have a natural metric; using it in your interpretations instead of "rate" or "expected count" is recommended. Here, "number of drinks". ::: ::: {.panel-tabset group="language"} ## Stata ::: {.callout-note icon="false" appearance="simple"} With [**mecompare**](https://www.trentonmize.com/software/mecompare/examples/model-types.html), can customize **start()** place of change, and the **amount(#)** of change. **uncenter** the change if you want an ME between those two exact \#s. ::: ```{.stata-run} . mecompare age, model(pmod) start(age=25) amount(5) uncenter Predicting: Predicted number of events Marginal effects (N_pmod=4983) | ME # Estimate SE P>|z| ---------------------------------+--------------------------------------- age + 5 (uncentered) | pmod | 1 -0.562 0.064 0.000 ``` ## R ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} avg_comparisons(pmod, variables = list(age = c(25, 30))) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` r-output Estimate Std. Error z Pr(>|z|) S 2.5 % 97.5 % -0.562 0.0636 -8.84 <0.001 59.9 -0.687 -0.438 Term: age Type: response Comparison: 30 - 25 ``` ::: ::: ::: > *Aging from 25 to 30 is associated with consuming about ½ a drink less per sitting (ME = -0.562; p \< 0.001).* ## Probabilities of specific counts - For a given rate, the probability of count *j* for observation *i* is: $$\Pr(y_{i} = j\,|\,\mathbf{x}_{i}) = \frac{e^{-\widehat{\mu}_{i}}\,\widehat{\mu}_{i}^{\,j}}{j!}$$ - Sometimes the probability of specific count is of interest - Pr(*y* = 0) is commonly of interest - Depending on research question, probabilities at other values and/or cumulative probabilities may be of interest - E.g., To determine who is at risk, examine what the probability is that someone consumes ≥ 4 drinks in a typical sitting: Pr(*y* ≥ 4) - Probabilities are also used to assess the adequacy of the model ### Plotting probabilities of specific counts ::: {.panel-tabset group="language"} ## Stata - In Stata, can request the probability of a specific count \# on **margins**, with option **predict(pr(#))** - And a range with **predict(pr(#,#))** ```{.stata-run} . *6.4.i - Pr(y=0) . est restore pmod (results pmod are active now) . qui margins, at(age=(21(1)35) woman=(0 1)) predict(pr(0)) . marginsplot, recastci(rline) ciopts(lpat(dash) col(gs12)) ylab(0(.1).4) xlab(2 > 1(2)35) /// > ytitle("Pr(Typically Consumes 0 Drinks)") xtitle("Age in Years") /// > title("[6.4.i] Probability of Consuming Zero Drinks in a Typical Sitting", > size(medium)) Variables that uniquely identify margins: age woman ``` ![](fig/cda-06_04_i-drinks-10.png){width=80% fig-alt="[6.4.i] Probability of typically consuming zero drinks by age, with confidence intervals: it rises with age for both groups, from about 0.03 at 21 to 0.17 at 35 for men and from about 0.11 to 0.33 for women."} ## R - In R, **plot_predictions** only predicts the expected count - Instead, use **predictions()** first and convert each person's predicted count to the probability of a specific count with **dpois(#, x)** inside the **hypothesis** option - Take the **mean()** to average within each age and gender combination - Use **ggplot** to make the graph using the stored predictions ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # 6.4.i - Pr(y=0) pr0 <- predictions(pmod, type = "response", newdata = datagrid(age = 21:35, woman = unique, grid_type = "counterfactual"), hypothesis = ~ I(mean(dpois(0, x))) | age + woman) ggplot(pr0, aes(age, estimate, ymin = conf.low, ymax = conf.high, color = woman, fill = woman)) + geom_ribbon(alpha = .2, color = NA) + geom_line() + scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(21, 35, 2)) + scale_y_continuous(breaks = seq(0, .4, .1), limits = c(0, .4)) + labs(title = "[6.4.i] Probability of Consuming Zero Drinks in a Typical Sitting", x = "Age in Years", y = "Pr(Typically Consumes 0 Drinks)", color = NULL, fill = NULL) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](6-4-poisson-example_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-10-1.png){fig-alt='[6.4.i] Probability of typically consuming zero drinks by age, with confidence intervals: it rises with age for both groups, from about 0.03 at 21 to 0.17 at 35 for men and from about 0.11 to 0.33 for women.' width=80%} ::: ::: ::: ### Marginal effects on probabilities of specific counts - Define $\eta$ as the probability of a specific count \# (or range) $$\eta = \Pr(y = j\,|\,\mathbf{x}_{i}) = \frac{e^{-\widehat{\mu}_{i}}\,\widehat{\mu}_{i}^{\,j}}{j!}$$ - Marginal effect is difference in probability of specific count, conditional on two values of the focal IV of interest $$ME = \eta(x_{k} = end,\, \mathbf{x}_{-k} = \mathbf{x}^{*}) - \eta(x_{k} = start,\, \mathbf{x}_{-k} = \mathbf{x}^{*})$$ > ***Interpretation:** The difference in the probability of a count of \# for a change in x~k~ of δ, holding other independent variables constant* - And for a range of counts > ***Interpretation:** The difference in the probability of a count between \# and \# for a change in x~k~ of δ, holding other independent variables constant* ::: {.panel-tabset group="language"} ## Stata ```{.stata-run} . *NOTE: Pass customized predict() functions . mecompare age, model(pmod) amount(trimrange) predict(pr(0)) Predicting: Pr(drinktime=0) Marginal effects (N_pmod=4983) | ME # Estimate SE P>|z| ---------------------------------+--------------------------------------- age(5-95%) | pmod | 1 0.065 0.007 0.000 ``` ## R ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} avg_comparisons(pmod, variables = list(age = c(26, 31)), comparison = function(hi, lo) dpois(0, hi) - dpois(0, lo)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` r-output Estimate Std. Error z Pr(>|z|) S 2.5 % 97.5 % 0.0654 0.00712 9.18 <0.001 64.4 0.0514 0.0793 Term: age Type: response Comparison: custom ``` ::: ::: ::: > *Aging from the 5^th^ to 95^th^ percentile in the data (26 to 31), predicts a 6.5 percentage point increase in the probability of not drinking any alcoholic drinks.* ::: {.callout-note icon="false" appearance="simple"} **Interpretation tip**: As with a +SD effect, the first time you report a (trimmed) range ME, useful to remind readers what those values are in your data. ::: ::: {.panel-tabset group="language"} ## Stata ```{.stata-run} . *6.4.j - Pr(y=3) . est restore pmod (results pmod are active now) . qui margins, at(age=(21(1)35) woman=(0 1)) predict(pr(3)) . marginsplot, recastci(rline) ciopts(lpat(dash) col(gs12)) ylab(0(.1).4) xlab(2 > 1(2)35) /// > ytitle("Pr(Typically Consumes 3 Drinks)") xtitle("Age in Years") /// > title("[6.4.j] Probability of Consuming Three Drinks in a Typical Sitting" > , size(medium)) Variables that uniquely identify margins: age woman ``` ![](fig/cda-06_04_j-drinks-11.png){width=80% fig-alt="[6.4.j] Probability of typically consuming three drinks by age, with confidence intervals: for men it is about 0.19 to 0.21 and peaks in the mid-20s before falling to about 0.16 at 35; for women it falls from about 0.19 at 21 to 0.08 at 35."} ## R ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # 6.4.j - Pr(y=3) pr3 <- predictions(pmod, type = "response", newdata = datagrid(age = 21:35, woman = unique, grid_type = "counterfactual"), hypothesis = ~ I(mean(dpois(3, x))) | age + woman) ggplot(pr3, aes(age, estimate, ymin = conf.low, ymax = conf.high, color = woman, fill = woman)) + geom_ribbon(alpha = .2, color = NA) + geom_line() + scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(21, 35, 2)) + scale_y_continuous(breaks = seq(0, .4, .1), limits = c(0, .4)) + labs(title = "[6.4.j] Probability of Consuming Three Drinks in a Typical Sitting", x = "Age in Years", y = "Pr(Typically Consumes 3 Drinks)", color = NULL, fill = NULL) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](6-4-poisson-example_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-12-1.png){fig-alt='[6.4.j] Probability of typically consuming three drinks by age, with confidence intervals: for men it is about 0.19 to 0.21 and peaks in the mid-20s before falling to about 0.16 at 35; for women it falls from about 0.19 at 21 to 0.08 at 35.' width=80%} ::: ::: ::: ::: {.panel-tabset group="language"} ## Stata ```{.stata-run} . *6.4.k - Pr(y >= 4) . qui margins, at(age=(21(1)35) woman=(0 1)) predict(pr(4,18)) . marginsplot, recastci(rline) ciopts(lpat(dash) col(gs12)) ylab(0(.1).7) xlab(2 > 1(2)35) /// > ytitle("Pr(Typically Consumes 4+ Drinks)") xtitle("Age in Years") /// > title("[6.4.k] Probability of Consuming Four or More Drinks in a Typical S > itting", size(medium)) Variables that uniquely identify margins: age woman ``` ![](fig/cda-06_04_k-drinks-13.png){width=80% fig-alt="[6.4.k] Probability of typically consuming four or more drinks by age, with confidence intervals: it falls with age, from about 0.52 at 21 to 0.13 at 35 for men and from about 0.22 to 0.04 for women."} ## R - In R, for a range of counts, use **ppois(#, x)**, which gives the probability of \# or fewer. Specify amount between *end \#* and *start \# -- 1*. E.g.
